notes.23.1.1: 'elidunt' ('dash, squeeze out'): forcing boy-mediums to speak oracles is the usual reading; some take it as killing boys to get an oracle.
notes.23.4.1: 'Who are cured by belching' (qui ructando curantur) is obscure. Socordius, Tenatius and Asclepiodotus are not identified.

nodes.text: And so we say that certain spiritual substances exist. Nor is the name new. The philosophers know of demons, since Socrates himself waited on the decision of a demon. And why not? For a demon is said to have attached itself to him from boyhood, one that plainly dissuaded him from the good.

All the poets know them; even the unlearned common people use [the word] often in cursing. For with the same word of execration it also names Satan, the chief of this evil race, out of the soul's own awareness. Angels too even Plato did not deny.

Even the magicians are at hand as witnesses to both names. But how, out of certain angels corrupted of their own free will, a still more corrupt race of demons came forth, condemned by God together with the authors of their race and with the prince we mentioned, is learned in its order from the sacred writings.

For now it will be enough to set out their activity. Their activity is the overthrow of man. So spiritual wickedness made its very first beginning in man's destruction. Accordingly, they inflict on bodies diseases and certain bitter mishaps, and on the soul sudden and extraordinary fits of violence. Their subtlety and thinness give them the means to reach both substances of a man.

Spiritual powers can do a great deal, so that, being invisible and imperceptible, they appear in their effect rather than in their action: as when some hidden blight in the air brings down fruit and crops in the flower, kills them in the bud, wounds them as they ripen; or as when the air, tampered with in some unseen way, pours out its pestilential draughts.

With the same hidden contagion, then, the breath of demons and angels also works corruption of the mind, with frenzies and foul insanities or savage lusts, along with errors of every kind; and the chief of these is the error by which it commends these gods of yours to the captured and ensnared minds of men, so as to procure for itself its own proper food of savour and blood, offered to statues and images.
And what pasture does it seek more carefully than to turn man away from the thought of the true divinity by false illusions? How it works these too, I shall explain.

Every spirit is winged. This is what angels and demons are. Therefore they are everywhere in a moment; the whole world is one place to them; what is being done where, they know as easily as they report it. Their speed is believed to be divinity, because their substance is unknown. So they sometimes want to be seen as the authors of the things they report. And indeed they sometimes are, of evils; of good things, never.

God's dispositions too they overheard back then, when the prophets preached them, and now they pick them up as the readings resound. So, taking from here certain lots of the times, they imitate divinity while they steal divination.

As for oracles, with what skill they temper their ambiguities to fit the outcome, the Croesuses know, the Pyrrhuses know. Again, the Pythian announced that a tortoise was being boiled down with the flesh of a sheep in the way we described above: in a moment he had been in Lydia. From dwelling in the air, and from their nearness to the stars, and from their dealings with the clouds, they are able to know the preparations of the sky, so that they also promise rains which they already feel coming.

Very kind they are, to be sure, in the care of illnesses as well. For first they do harm, then they prescribe remedies, novel or contrary to the point of miracle, after which they stop doing harm, and are believed to have healed.

Further: if magicians too produce phantoms and dishonour the souls of the dead; if they force boys into oracular speech; if they play out many marvels with the tricks of street conjurers; if they also send dreams, having at their side the power of angels and demons once invited, through whom even goats and tables have been accustomed to divine: how much more will that power, of its own will and for its own business, strive with all its strength to do what it performs for another's business!

But enough of words; from here on, a demonstration of the thing itself, by which we shall show that both names have one and the same nature. Let someone be brought forward here, right before your tribunals, who is agreed to be driven by a demon. Ordered to speak by any Christian you like, that spirit will confess itself a demon as truly as elsewhere it falsely calls itself a lord.

Likewise let someone be produced from those who are thought to be possessed by a god, who, breathing over the altars, conceive the deity from the smoke, who are cured by belching, who prophesy by panting.

That very Virgin Caelestis, promiser of rains, that very Aesculapius, revealer of medicines, supplier to Socordius and Tenatius and Asclepiodotus, who were to die another day: if they do not confess themselves demons, not daring to lie to a Christian, then and there shed the blood of that most impudent Christian!
